original_question: What produces gamma-ray-burst emission above 100 MeV, especially the frequent delay of Large Area Telescope (LAT) photons relative to the lower-energy prompt emission, the long-lived GeV decay phase, and the varying spectral relation between the GeV and MeV bands? The explanation must determine whether the high-energy signal is internal, external-shock afterglow emission, or a superposition of multiple components.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the focus on emission above 100 MeV, the observed delayed onset of LAT photons relative to lower-energy prompt emission, the long-lived GeV decay phase after the GBM-band prompt emission, the varying spectral relation (single Band vs. multi-component spectra) between the GeV and MeV bands, and the need to determine whether the high-energy emission arises from internal dissipation, external-shock afterglow, or a superposition of multiple components.
missing_details: Explicit definitions of Fermi LAT and GBM instruments and their respective energy ranges (LAT >100 MeV; GBM ∼8 keV–40 MeV)
Specification of the sample size and detection rate (e.g., 17 LAT-detected GRBs before May 2010; ∼9 detections per year)
Quantitative values for typical onset delays (on the order of seconds) and the power-law decay slope of the long-lived GeV emission (∼−1.4)

Definitions and notation for the spectral components (Band function with indices α and β and peak energy E_p; thermal-like BB component; extra PL component) and examples of GRBs exhibiting each combination
Clear separation of prompt (GBM-band) and afterglow (LAT-band) phases with respective observational windows
Physical descriptions of ‘internal’ emission versus ‘external shock’ emission and criteria for distinguishing between them
Mention of specific GRB examples (e.g., GRB 080916C, GRB 090902B, GRB 090510) to illustrate the observed phenomena
refined_question: Based on Fermi LAT and GBM observations of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), what is the physical origin of emission above 100 MeV? Specifically, how can one explain (i) the delayed onset of >100 MeV photons detected by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) relative to prompt emission in the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) band, (ii) the long-lived LAT-band emission that decays as a power law (slope ∼−1.4) after the GBM-band prompt phase ceases, and (iii) the diverse spectral behavior—ranging from a single Band function spanning keV to GeV energies to the presence of thermal-like and extra power-law components—between the MeV and GeV regimes? Determine whether the >100 MeV emission is produced by internal dissipation within the relativistic jet, by external-forward-shock afterglow processes, or by a superposition of multiple emission components.
justification: The paper identifies this open problem under Section 2.9 ‘Origin of high energy emission’ (p. 216), which summarizes key observational properties of Fermi-LAT detected GRBs above 100 MeV, including delayed onset (property 1), single vs. multi-component spectra (properties 2–5), temporal tracking and internal origin during prompt phase (property 6), and the long-lived GeV decay favoring external shock or superposition (property 7) [Section 2.9, p. 216–217]. The refined question reproduces these elements exactly, adds necessary domain-specific definitions (instrument names, energy ranges, spectral model notation, sample statistics, decay slope), and frames the choices among internal dissipation, external-shock afterglow, and multiple-component superposition as in the paper’s discussion.
